summary: Defines a backward-compatible extension to IS-IS that adds a three-way handshake when point-to-point adjacencies come up. IS-IS originally relied on reliable links and used no such handshake. The extension also improves robustness and works with systems that do not support it. It was replaced by RFC 5303.

eli5.summary: Two people shaking hands should both confirm they are really connected. This adds an extra confirmation step to the way two IS-IS routers link up.

subtitle: Confirming both directions of a routing link with a three-way handshake

tldr.problem: IS-IS routing assumes reliable point-to-point links and uses only a two-way handshake, but this can fail if a link becomes one-directional or if messages are lost, leaving databases unsynchronized for hours.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3373 adds a three-way handshake extension where routers exchange their current handshake state, confirming that both directions of the link are working before declaring the adjacency up. The extension also provides unique circuit IDs to support more than 256 interfaces.
tldr.outcome: The extension is backward compatible with existing IS-IS systems and has been implemented by multiple vendors, improving robustness of IS-IS networks on unreliable links.

today: RFC 3373 was replaced by RFC 5303, which consolidates IS-IS specifications. The three-way handshake extension defined here became part of the standard IS-IS behavior and is widely implemented in modern routers to ensure robust operation on unreliable links.

sections.title: IS-IS and Reliable Links
sections.content:
The IS-IS routing protocol was designed with the assumption that point-to-point links are reliable and that messages sent on one direction of the link will be received in the other. Under this assumption, IS-IS uses a simple two-way handshake: each router sends a Hello packet to its neighbor and waits to hear a Hello back. Once each hears the other's Hello, both declare the adjacency up and synchronize their routing databases.

However, in real networks, links can fail in only one direction—a router might transmit successfully to its neighbor but receive nothing back, or vice versa. Additionally, if a Complete Sequence Number PDU (CSNP) used for database synchronization is lost, the databases could remain out of sync for a very long time (up to 18 hours). These failures can cause incorrect routing decisions and traffic loss.
sections.eli5: IS-IS routing assumes links always work both ways. But sometimes a link breaks so that one direction works while the other doesn't, and the protocol doesn't notice.

sections.title: The Three-Way Handshake Extension
sections.content:
The RFC defines a backward-compatible optional mechanism added to IS-IS Hello packets. Each router reports its current three-way handshake state: Down (not hearing from the neighbor), Initializing (hearing from the neighbor but unsure if the neighbor hears it back), or Up (both routers confirm they hear each other). Each router also sends its own extended circuit ID and, when known, the neighbor's system ID and extended circuit ID.

When a router receives a Hello with this new option, it checks whether the neighbor has correctly identified the local router's ID and circuit ID. If the neighbor identifies the wrong circuit, the routers know they are not directly connected and discard the packet. This protects against the case where multiple routers receive the same signal from a misconfigured link or a physical layer broadcast that was not supposed to happen.
sections.eli5: Each router tells the other: "I hear you as neighbor X on circuit Y, do you hear me?" If the neighbor says yes and confirms the right circuit, then the link is good.

sections.title: State Transitions and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC defines state transitions based on what each router observes. Both routers start in the Down state. When one hears from the other, it moves to Initializing. When both routers have heard from each other and confirmed the correct circuit IDs, both move to the Up state. A state transition table determines when adjacency state changes occur.

The extension is fully backward compatible: systems that do not support the three-way handshake simply ignore the new option in Hello packets and continue using the old two-way handshake procedure. A router that supports the extension will only apply the three-way logic if both sides include the new option in their Hellos. This allows new and old IS-IS implementations to coexist in the same network.
sections.eli5: At first both say "Down." When one hears from the other, it says "Initializing." When both have said hello back correctly, both say "Up." Old routers that don't understand the new way still work fine.

sections.title: Support for Many Interfaces
sections.content:
IS-IS traditionally limited systems to 256 point-to-point interfaces because the local circuit ID was an 8-bit field. However, modern routers need to support many more interfaces. The RFC solves this by defining an extended local circuit ID, a 32-bit field that allows unique identification of many more circuits.

The extended circuit ID is assigned when a circuit is created and remains unique for that circuit on the router. Relying on extended circuit IDs rather than the 8-bit local circuit ID for the three-way handshake allows the protocol to support many more interfaces without ambiguity or collision risk.
sections.eli5: The old circuit ID was only 8 bits, allowing at most 256 interfaces. The new extended circuit ID is 32 bits, so a router can have thousands of interfaces.
